questions.q: Why do computers use a *hierarchy* of memory technologies instead of one kind of memory?
choices: No single technology is simultaneously fast, cheap per byte, and large in capacity, so several are combined at different points on the trade-off
Operating systems require at least three kinds of memory to boot
DRAM cannot be addressed by the CPU directly, so SRAM must translate for it
Disks are faster than RAM for large files, so both are needed
questions.explain: Memory has three competing properties: **speed, cost, capacity**, and like the project-management triangle you can only "pick two." Fast memory is costly in quantity; cheap large memory must be slow. The hierarchy puts a little fast/expensive storage near the CPU and lots of slow/cheap storage further away, and locality lets programs get close to the speed of the top at close to the cost of the bottom.

questions.q: Moving **down** the memory hierarchy (from registers toward remote storage), which of the following generally increase? Select all that apply.
choices: Capacity
Access latency
Cost per byte
Size of the unit transferred between adjacent levels
Speed
questions.explain: Lower levels are **larger, slower, and cheaper per byte**. The transfer unit also grows: words (L1→L0), 64-byte cache lines (between SRAM levels and DRAM), ~4 KB pages/disk blocks (disk→memory), whole files (remote→local). Cost per byte and speed *decrease* going down.

questions.q: In the CS:APP pyramid, what does main memory (L4, DRAM) hold, and where does it get it from?
choices: Disk blocks retrieved from local disks
Cache lines retrieved from L3
Words retrieved from registers
Files retrieved from remote servers
questions.explain: Each level holds data retrieved from the level **below** it: registers hold words from cache, L1–L3 hold cache lines from the next level down, **main memory holds disk blocks from local disks**, and local disks hold files from remote servers.

questions.q: The central idea of the hierarchy is that the device at level *k* acts as a cache for level *k+1*. Which is an example of that idea at the **L5/L6** boundary?
choices: A web browser keeping copies of recently visited pages on the local disk
The L1 cache keeping copies of recently used DRAM lines
The CPU keeping loop counters in registers
DRAM refreshing its rows every 64 ms
questions.explain: L5 is local secondary storage and L6 is remote storage. A **browser cache** (or Dropbox's synced copies, or an NFS client cache) keeps local-disk copies of remote data to avoid repeated slow network trips — local disk caching remote storage. The L1/DRAM option is a cache relationship too, but at a different boundary.

questions.q: Why are data moved between lower levels (e.g., disk → memory) in much **bigger** chunks than between upper levels (e.g., L1 → registers)?
choices: Lower levels have long access latency, so each slow access fetches a big block to amortize that cost over many bytes — which pays off because of spatial locality
Lower levels have wider buses, so they cannot transfer small amounts
Big chunks reduce the total capacity needed at the upper level
The operating system forbids transfers smaller than a page
questions.explain: Finding the first byte on a slow device is the expensive part; the neighbouring bytes are almost free. Bringing in a large block spreads the latency across many bytes, and since programs tend to use nearby data soon (**spatial locality**), those extra bytes are usually useful.

questions.q: What does "random access" mean in random-access memory?
choices: Any item can be reached in (roughly) constant time, regardless of its location or what was accessed before
Data is stored at random addresses chosen by the hardware
Items must be accessed in a random order to be efficient
Access time grows with the distance from the last address read
questions.explain: On a random-access device the address is decoded and the cell is selected directly — no traversal. Contrast a **sequential** medium like tape, where you must pass everything in between. Hard disks sit in between: position-dependent mechanical delays mean they are *not* truly random-access.

questions.q: A hard disk drive is a random-access memory device, because its access time is the same for every sector.
questions.explain: HDD access time depends on where the head currently is (**seek**) and where the platter is in its rotation (**rotational latency**). It is a block device with position-dependent latency, not RAM.

questions.q: Why is RAM (both SRAM and DRAM) **volatile**?
choices: Its bits are electrical states that must be actively maintained — leaking capacitor charge or a powered feedback loop — which disappear without power
It is erased by the operating system at shutdown
Its magnetic grains lose alignment when the platter stops
It stores electrons behind an insulator, which slowly tunnel out
questions.explain: A DRAM bit is charge on a capacitor that leaks within milliseconds; an SRAM bit is a transistor feedback loop that only exists while current flows. **Non-volatile** storage (disks, flash) stores bits as physical states that persist unpowered — magnetized grains or electrons trapped behind oxide (the last option describes flash, which retains data for years).

questions.q: A DRAM cell consists of one transistor and one capacitor. What role does each play?
choices: The capacitor stores the bit (charged = 1, discharged = 0); the transistor is the access switch that lets the bit be read, written, or refreshed
The transistor stores the bit; the capacitor amplifies it when read
The capacitor keeps time with the system clock; the transistor stores the bit
Both store half of the bit, so two cells make one byte
questions.explain: In the **1T1C** cell the capacitor holds the charge that represents the bit. The transistor acts as the gate to the capacitor: opening it lets charge flow out (read), lets the capacitor be charged/drained (write), and lets it be topped up (refresh).

questions.q: What does the word **dynamic** in DRAM refer to?
choices: The capacitors leak charge, so every cell must be constantly re-read and rewritten (refreshed) to keep its value
DRAM can change its capacity dynamically as programs request memory
DRAM changes its clock speed dynamically with load
Data moves dynamically between DRAM chips to balance wear
questions.explain: The dielectric isn't a perfect insulator and the transistor isn't a perfect "off" switch, so charge leaks away. DRAM must be **refreshed** constantly (JEDEC: every cell at least once per 64 ms). Refresh opens a row, sense amplifiers restore each cell's faint voltage to a clean 0/1, and the values are written back. SRAM needs none of this — hence *static*.

questions.q: JEDEC requires every DRAM cell to be refreshed at least once every **64 ms**. At that minimum rate, about how many times per second is each individual cell refreshed?
questions.explain: 1 s / 0.064 s = **15.625 ≈ 16 times per second** per cell. The chip as a whole is refreshed continuously, though: the controller issues ~8,192 refresh commands per 64 ms window (one every ~7.8 µs), each covering a group of rows. The slides' "hundreds of times per second" is loose shorthand for "constantly."

questions.q: Reading a DRAM cell is destructive: the value must be written back after every read.
questions.explain: The cell's tiny capacitor (~30 fF) shares its charge with the much larger bit line when the transistor opens, draining the cell. The **sense amplifier** detects and amplifies the value, then writes it back. This rewrite is one reason DRAM is slower than SRAM.

questions.q: How does an SRAM cell hold a bit without a capacitor or refresh?
choices: Its 4–6 transistors form a bistable circuit (two cross-coupled inverters) whose feedback loop holds either state as long as power is supplied
It stores the bit magnetically in the transistor gates
It traps electrons on a floating gate surrounded by oxide
It re-reads the bit from DRAM on every clock tick
questions.explain: Each inverter's output feeds the other's input: if A outputs 1, B outputs 0, which keeps A at 1. The loop sustains itself (like an inverted pendulum that falls to one side), so nothing leaks and no refresh is needed. Two more **access transistors** connect the cell to the bit lines.

questions.q: Because SRAM is *static* (never needs refresh), it is non-volatile and keeps its data when power is removed.
questions.explain: "Static" only means **no refresh while powered**. When power is cut the inverters stop driving and the state is lost, so SRAM is still **volatile**. Static ≠ non-volatile.

questions.q: Which statements correctly explain why caches use SRAM while main memory uses DRAM? Select all that apply.
choices: SRAM is faster because it avoids charging/discharging capacitors, refresh, and rewrite-after-read
An SRAM bit needs ~6 transistors vs. 1 transistor + 1 capacitor for DRAM, so SRAM is far less dense and much more expensive per bit
DRAM's density and low cost per bit make it suitable for large capacities
SRAM is non-volatile, so it is safer for cached data
DRAM is faster but too unstable for caches
questions.explain: This is the speed/cost/capacity trade-off: caches must be **fast** and can be **small**, so SRAM fits (≈10× faster than DRAM, ≈1000× cost per bit). Main memory must be **large and affordable**, so dense DRAM fits. Both are volatile, and DRAM is the slower of the two.

questions.q: Which statement about the L1/L2/L3 caches on a typical modern multicore CPU is correct?
choices: Each core has private L1 and L2; the L3 is larger, slower, and shared by all cores
L3 is the smallest and fastest, sitting closest to the ALU
All three levels are shared, and only registers are private
L1 is unified, while L2 and L3 are split into instruction and data caches
questions.explain: Moving toward the CPU, each level is **smaller and faster** and holds more frequently accessed data. L1 (split i/d) and L2 are per core; L3 (tens of MB on recent chips) is shared. L1 is the split one; L2 and L3 are unified.

questions.q: Why is the L1 cache split into an instruction cache and a data cache?
choices: So the CPU can fetch an instruction and a data word in the same cycle, and the two streams don't evict each other
Because instructions are stored in SRAM and data in DRAM
Because instructions are big-endian and data is little-endian
To make the L1 cache non-volatile for instructions
questions.explain: Separate i-cache and d-cache give two independent access paths every cycle and prevent a big data sweep from evicting the code of a hot loop (or vice versa). L2 and L3 are **unified**.

questions.q: What problem did asynchronous DRAM have, and how did SDRAM address it?
choices: Async DRAM ran on its own timing, so the CPU/controller often had to wait for it; SDRAM syncs to the system clock so data arrives on a known cycle, enabling pipelined commands and burst transfers
Async DRAM needed refresh; SDRAM eliminated refresh
Async DRAM was non-volatile; SDRAM made it volatile to increase speed
Async DRAM used capacitors; SDRAM replaced them with flip-flops
questions.explain: Before ~1992 DRAM carried out the memory controller's commands on its own schedule, creating a CPU–memory **bottleneck** that grew as CPUs got faster. With SDRAM the controller knows exactly which clock cycle data will appear on (the CAS latency), so it can issue new commands while earlier ones are in flight (**pipelining**) and receive several consecutive words on consecutive edges (**bursts**) — perfect for filling 64-byte cache lines. SDRAM still needs refresh.

questions.q: How does DDR SDRAM achieve double the data rate of original SDRAM at the same clock frequency?
choices: It transfers data on both the rising and the falling edge of each clock cycle
It uses two capacitors per bit
It doubles the clock frequency internally
It stores two bits per cell like MLC flash
questions.explain: Each clock cycle has a **rising** edge and a **falling** edge. Original SDRAM transferred on one; DDR transfers on **both**. That's why DDR speeds are quoted in MT/s (transfers per second) = 2 × the I/O clock. DDR2–DDR5 are successive improvements (more prefetch, lower voltage, higher rates).

questions.q: A DDR5-4800 memory channel transfers 4800 MT/s over a 64-bit (8-byte) bus. What is its peak bandwidth in **GB/s**?
questions.explain: Peak bandwidth = transfers/s × bytes per transfer = 4800 × 10⁶ × 8 B = **38.4 × 10⁹ B/s = 38.4 GB/s**. (Same method: DDR4-3200 → 25.6 GB/s.) The "4800" is already transfers per second, i.e. 2 × the 2400 MHz I/O clock.

questions.q: Why are CPU registers the fastest storage in the hierarchy?
choices: They are a small number of flip-flop cells built directly into the CPU's datapath, wired to the ALU with no bus trip needed
They are made of DRAM with an extra-fast refresh
They are the largest level, so data is always found there
They are non-volatile, so they never need to be reloaded
questions.explain: Registers sit right next to the ALU and are reached through internal wiring (**0 cycles** in the access table). There are very few of them (e.g. 16 GPRs on x86-64) — they are expensive, power-hungry, and optimized for speed rather than long-term retention or error checking, which is why we can't just build more.

questions.q: The slides say registers offer "minimal retention, error-checking, etc." What does this imply?
choices: Registers hold values only briefly for the current instructions and lack protections like ECC; anything that must be kept goes to memory or disk
Registers lose their values every clock cycle unless refreshed like DRAM
Registers can only be written once per program
Registers are unreliable and frequently corrupt data in normal use
questions.explain: Register contents are overwritten constantly, lost at power-off, and saved to memory by the OS on context switches. They're built for speed, not durable storage, so they carry little of the error-detection machinery server DRAM has.

questions.q: Which statements about local (L5) vs. remote (L6) secondary storage are correct? Select all that apply.
choices: Both are non-volatile
Local storage generally has lower latency and greater reliability because it doesn't depend on a network
Remote storage offers cost-effectiveness, scalability, and access from anywhere
Remote storage is faster than local storage because data centers use SSDs
A USB flash drive is an example of remote secondary storage
questions.explain: Secondary (permanent) storage is non-volatile and is the slowest, cheapest, most plentiful part of the hierarchy. **Local** devices (HDD, SSD, USB drives, optical discs) are directly connected. **Remote** storage (cloud, distributed file systems, web servers) adds network latency and fails if the network is down, but you rent capacity, scale on demand, and reach it anywhere.

questions.q: How does a hard disk drive store and read a bit?
choices: By magnetizing regions of grains on a spinning platter; the head reads the magnetic polarization (and writes by flipping it)
By trapping electrons on floating gates
By burning pits into a reflective layer read with a laser
By charging capacitors on the platter surface
questions.explain: The platter's ferromagnetic film holds regions whose magnetic orientation encodes data. The head's electromagnet flips orientation to write; a magnetoresistive sensor detects it to read. Magnetization persists without power → **non-volatile**. (Pits and lasers describe optical discs; floating gates describe flash.)

questions.q: All read/write heads in an HDD are mounted on one arm and move in unison. What is the set of tracks at the same radius across all surfaces called?
choices: A cylinder
A sector
A platter
A spindle
questions.explain: Because the heads move together, at any moment they're all over the same **cylinder**. A **track** is one ring on one surface; a **sector** is a fixed-size piece of a track (512 B or 4 KiB — the smallest read/write unit); the **spindle** spins all platters together.

questions.q: The three components of HDD access time are:
choices: Seek time, rotational latency, transfer time
Seek time, refresh time, CAS latency
Rotational latency, erase time, write amplification
Bus time, hit time, miss penalty
questions.explain: **Seek**: move the arm so the head is over the right track. **Rotational latency**: wait for the sector to spin under the head (on average half a revolution). **Transfer**: read/write the sector as it passes. T_access = T_seek + T_rotation + T_transfer.

questions.q: A disk spins at **15,000 RPM**, has an average seek time of **4 ms**, and averages **1,000 sectors per track**. Estimate the average time (in **ms**) to access one sector.
questions.explain: One revolution = 60 s / 15,000 = **4 ms**. Average rotational latency = ½ × 4 = **2 ms**. Transfer = 4 ms / 1,000 = **0.004 ms**. T_access = 4 + 2 + 0.004 = **6.004 ms** (≈ 6 ms). Note that seek + rotation dominate; transferring the sector is nearly free.

questions.q: What is the **average rotational latency**, in ms, of a 5,400 RPM disk?
questions.explain: One revolution = 60 s / 5,400 ≈ 11.11 ms. On average the target sector is half a revolution away, so average rotational latency = ½ × 11.11 ≈ **5.56 ms**.

questions.q: In a typical HDD access, which components dominate, and what quick estimate follows?
choices: Seek time and rotational latency dominate and are roughly equal, so ≈ 2 × seek time is a good estimate
Transfer time dominates, so bigger sectors make disks slower
Rotational latency alone dominates; seek time is negligible
All three are about equal, so ≈ 3 × transfer time is a good estimate
questions.explain: In the CS:APP example (7,200 RPM, 9 ms seek, 400 sectors/track): 9 + 4 + 0.02 ms. Finding the first byte is expensive; the rest of the sector is almost free. That's why disks and the OS move data in large blocks.

questions.q: A disk access takes **10 ms**. How many cycles is that on a **3 GHz** CPU, in **millions** of cycles?
questions.explain: 10 × 10⁻³ s × 3 × 10⁹ cycles/s = 3 × 10⁷ = **30 million cycles** — the "tens of millions of cycles" in the access-time table. One cycle at 3 GHz is ≈ 0.33 ns.

questions.q: In real NAND flash (the industry convention CS:APP follows), how are an erased cell and a programmed cell read?
choices: Erased (no trapped electrons) = 1, programmed (electrons trapped) = 0
Erased = 0, programmed = 1
Both read as 1; the difference is the voltage level only
Erased cells cannot be read until programmed
questions.explain: The slides simplify with "electrons present = 1," but the real convention is the reverse: erasing a block **sets all bits to 1**; programming traps electrons on the floating gate, raising the threshold voltage so the cell doesn't conduct → 0. The key idea either way: a bit is stored by the **presence or absence of trapped electrons**, which stay for years without power.

questions.q: Why is NAND flash called "NAND" even though its cells don't compute a NAND function?
choices: Cells are connected in series in strings, like the series transistors of a CMOS NAND gate — a string conducts only if all its cells conduct
Each cell outputs the NAND of its two neighbours
It stands for "Non-volatile And"
It was invented by the same company that invented the NAND gate
questions.explain: The resemblance is structural: series-connected cells, like NAND's "output 0 only if all inputs are 1." The cell stores rather than computes, hence "resembles a NAND gate but does not function like one." **NOR flash** wires cells in parallel (byte-level random reads, lower density).

questions.q: A flash page cannot be overwritten in place. What must happen instead, and what is the consequence?
choices: The whole block containing it must be erased first, so the controller copies still-valid pages elsewhere and erases the block — writing more than the host requested (write amplification)
The page is refreshed like DRAM, which slows reads
The head must seek to a new track, adding latency
The page is marked read-only forever
questions.explain: Flash reads/writes in **pages** but erases only whole **blocks** of many pages. Changing one page may force copying the block's other valid pages to a fresh block and erasing the old one — **write amplification**. This accelerates wear, which is why controllers use wear leveling, garbage collection, and TRIM.

questions.q: Which are genuine **advantages** of SSDs over HDDs? Select all that apply.
choices: No seek time or rotational latency, so access is tens of µs instead of ~10 ms
Lower power use
Less prone to mechanical failure (no spinning platters or head crashes)
Unlimited write endurance
Easier data recovery after failure or deletion
Lower cost per byte
questions.explain: SSDs have **no moving parts**: faster, lower power, rugged. But cells **wear out** after limited program/erase cycles, **data recovery is much harder**, and cost per byte is higher than HDDs.

questions.q: What is the purpose of **wear leveling** in an SSD controller?
choices: To spread erase cycles evenly across all blocks so no block wears out early
To keep the platters spinning at a constant speed
To refresh leaking cells like DRAM
To encrypt data so it cannot be recovered
questions.explain: Each program/erase cycle stresses the tunnel oxide, and cells survive only ~100–100,000 cycles depending on type (SLC best, QLC worst). The flash translation layer remaps logical blocks so erases are distributed uniformly, greatly extending drive life.

questions.q: Why is recovering deleted or lost data much harder on an SSD than on an HDD?
choices: TRIM and garbage collection actively erase freed blocks, the flash translation layer scatters data across chips, and controllers often scramble or encrypt data
SSDs store data magnetically at a smaller scale
SSDs are volatile and lose data when unplugged
SSDs overwrite deleted files with zeros on every boot
questions.explain: On an HDD, a deleted file's magnetic data usually remains until overwritten, and platters can be read in a lab. On an SSD the drive itself erases freed blocks ahead of time, and without the controller's mapping tables the raw NAND contents are very hard to reassemble.

questions.q: Which ordering of approximate access times matches the course's table?
choices: Registers 0 cycles; cache 4–75 cycles; RAM hundreds of cycles; disk tens of millions of cycles
Registers 4 cycles; cache hundreds; RAM thousands; disk millions
Registers 0 cycles; cache hundreds; RAM tens of millions; disk billions
Registers, cache, and RAM all take the same time because they are all RAM
questions.explain: Each step down costs roughly one to several **orders of magnitude**. If one cycle were one second: L1 ≈ 4 s, DRAM ≈ 4 min, SSD ≈ 2–3 days, HDD ≈ a year. That enormous gap is why predicting what's needed next (locality) matters so much.

questions.q: Define the two kinds of locality.
choices: Temporal: an address accessed now is likely to be accessed again soon. Spatial: addresses near one just accessed are likely to be accessed soon
Temporal: nearby addresses are accessed soon. Spatial: the same address is accessed again soon
Temporal: data is accessed in the order it was written. Spatial: data is spread across many devices
Temporal: the program runs quickly. Spatial: the program uses little memory
questions.explain: **Temporal** = same address, again, soon (reuse). **Spatial** = nearby addresses soon (neighbours). Caches exploit temporal locality by keeping recently used lines, and spatial locality by fetching whole lines.

choices: Spatial locality (stride-1)
Temporal locality only
Both temporal and spatial locality, since each element is used many times
Neither, since each element is used only once
questions.explain: Each `v[i]` is touched **once**, so there's no temporal reuse of elements — but consecutive elements live at consecutive addresses (**stride-1**), which is good spatial locality. By contrast `sum`, `i`, and `n` show **temporal** locality (used every iteration), and the loop's instructions show **both** (reused and contiguous).

questions.q: In the same `sumvec` loop, which items exhibit **temporal** locality? Select all that apply.
choices: The variable `sum`
The loop counter `i`
The loop's instructions
The individual elements `v[i]`
questions.explain: `sum` and `i` are referenced on every iteration, and the few loop-body instructions execute repeatedly (they also sit at consecutive addresses, giving spatial locality). Each array element is used only once, so it contributes spatial, not temporal, locality.

questions.q: At the **operating-system** level, how is the principle of locality exploited?
choices: RAM is used as a cache for the disk: recently referenced pages are kept in memory (paging / virtual memory) to avoid slow disk accesses
The OS rewrites programs so their loops are stride-1
The OS stores all files in L3 cache
The OS converts all data to big-endian for faster access
questions.explain: Locality is exploited at three layers: **hardware** (caches hold recently used blocks), **OS** (RAM caches disk via 4 KB pages; a page fault loads a missing page, possibly evicting another), and **applications** (programmers write code that maximizes locality).

questions.q: A 3×3 matrix with elements a00…a22 is stored in **row-major** order. What is its layout in memory?
questions.explain: Row-major stores each **row** contiguously, one after another (C, C++, Java, NumPy default). The second option is **column-major** (Fortran, MATLAB, Julia, R).

questions.q: `int a[4][6];` is stored in row-major order starting at address **0x3000** (`sizeof(int)` = 4). What is the address of `a[2][5]`? (Answer in hex, e.g. `0x1234`.)
questions.explain: &a[i][j] = base + (i × C + j) × sizeof(T) = 0x3000 + (2 × 6 + 5) × 4 = 0x3000 + 17 × 4 = 0x3000 + 68. 68 = 0x44, so the address is **0x3044**. The i × C term skips i whole rows of C elements.

questions.q: In a row-major language, a program sums a 3×3 matrix with the **column** index in the *outer* loop and the row index in the *inner* loop. In what order are storage positions 0–8 visited, and what is the stride?
questions.explain: Going down a column moves from a[i][j] to a[i+1][j], skipping a whole row of C = 3 elements: positions 0, 3, 6, then wrap to 1, 4, 7, then 2, 5, 8. That's a **stride-3** pattern (stride = number of columns). Row-wise traversal would be stride-1, matching storage order — better spatial locality.

questions.q: `double d[8][10];` is stored row-major. A loop traverses it **column by column** (row index in the inner loop). What is the stride in **bytes** between consecutive accesses? (`sizeof(double)` = 8)
questions.explain: Column-wise traversal of a row-major R × C array is **stride-C** in elements: here C = 10, so stride-10. In bytes: 10 × 8 = **80 bytes**. (Note it's the number of *columns* that matters, not rows.)

questions.q: You're writing a nested loop over a large 2-D array in **Fortran** (column-major). Which loop order gives the best spatial locality?
choices: Row index in the inner loop (walk down each column)
Column index in the inner loop (walk across each row)
Either — Fortran arrays have no layout in memory
Diagonal traversal
questions.explain: In column-major storage each **column** is contiguous, so varying the row index fastest walks memory with **stride-1**. It's the mirror image of C/C++, where the column index should vary fastest. The rule: make the inner loop follow the storage order.

questions.q: On real hardware with 64-byte cache lines, the row-wise and column-wise sums of the lecture's 3×3 `int` matrix run at essentially the same speed. Why?
choices: The whole matrix is 36 bytes, which fits in a single cache line, so both loops miss once and then hit
Modern compilers always make both loops stride-1
Caches don't exist for arrays smaller than a page
3×3 matrices are stored in registers, not memory
questions.explain: 9 ints × 4 B = 36 B < 64 B, so one line fetch brings in everything (assuming it doesn't straddle a line boundary). The stride difference only matters when the matrix is much larger than a line — and dramatically so when a column's lines exceed the cache.

questions.q: `int m[1024][1024]` (row-major, 4 MB) is summed **column-wise** on a CPU with a 32 KB L1 data cache and 64-byte lines. Why does nearly every access miss in L1?
choices: Each access is 4,096 bytes from the previous, landing in a different line; one column touches 1,024 lines (64 KB), more than L1 holds, so lines are evicted before the loop comes back to use their other 15 ints
The matrix is stored column-major in C, so the loop is actually stride-1
Column-wise access disables the cache
Each int spans two cache lines
questions.explain: Stride = 1,024 ints = 4,096 B ≥ the 64 B line, so every access touches a new line. By the time the loop moves to column j+1, the line holding m[0][j+1] has been evicted → miss rate ≈ 100% (capacity misses). Row-wise, the same code misses only once per 16 ints (≈ 6.25%), and hardware prefetchers hide much of that.

questions.q: An array of 4-byte `int`s far larger than the cache is read once with a **stride of 4 elements** (every 4th int). With 64-byte cache lines and a cold cache, approximately what **percentage** of accesses miss?
questions.explain: Each line holds 64 / 4 = 16 ints. Stepping 4 ints (16 bytes) at a time gives 64 / 16 = 4 accesses per line: 1 miss + 3 hits → **25%** miss rate. General rule for stride-k with k × sizeof(T) < line size: miss rate ≈ (k × sizeof(T)) / line size = 16/64. Stride-1 would give 4/64 = 6.25%; a stride ≥ 16 ints gives 100%.

questions.q: A classmate argues: "RAM has constant-time access, so the order in which my program touches memory can't affect its speed." What's the best rebuttal?
choices: Constant time holds only within one RAM device; a load goes through L1 → L2 → L3 → DRAM (→ disk), so latency depends on *where* the data currently is, and access order determines that
RAM isn't really constant-time; DRAM addresses near 0 are faster
The order only matters on big-endian machines
The order matters because the CPU executes loops backwards
questions.explain: The issue isn't *which* items you access but **where in the hierarchy** they are when you ask: ~4 cycles in L1, 200+ from DRAM, millions if paged in from disk. Every trip to slower memory also costs **bus time** on a shared, bandwidth-limited bus. Good locality keeps data in cache; poor locality forces misses.

questions.q: The CPU requests the 4-byte int at address **0x1014**. With 64-byte aligned cache lines, what is brought into the cache on a miss?
choices: The entire 64-byte line 0x1000–0x103F
Only the 4 bytes 0x1014–0x1017
The 64 bytes 0x1014–0x1053
The whole 4 KB page containing 0x1014
questions.explain: Caches always fetch a **whole line**, and lines are aligned: the line containing address A starts at A rounded down to a multiple of 64 (clear the low 6 bits): 0x1014 → 0x1000. The neighbouring 15 ints arrive "for free," which is how caches exploit spatial locality. (Pages are the disk↔memory unit, not the cache unit.)

questions.q: With **64-byte** aligned cache lines, what is the starting address of the line containing address **0x2A7C**? (Answer in hex.)
questions.explain: Round down to a multiple of 64 = 0x40, i.e. clear the low 6 bits. 0x7C = 0111 1100; clearing the low 6 bits leaves 0100 0000 = 0x40. So the line starts at **0x2A40** and spans 0x2A40–0x2A7F.

questions.q: A program makes 2,000 memory references and 70 of them miss in the cache. What is the **hit rate**, as a percentage?
questions.explain: Miss rate = misses / references = 70 / 2,000 = 3.5%. Every reference either hits or misses, so hit rate = 1 − miss rate = **96.5%**.

questions.q: A cache has a hit time of **2 cycles**, a miss rate of **5%**, and a miss penalty of **150 cycles**. What is the average memory access time in cycles?
questions.explain: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty = 2 + 0.05 × 150 = 2 + 7.5 = **9.5 cycles**. Even a small miss rate dominates because the penalty is so large.

questions.q: A cache has a hit time of **1 ns** and a miss penalty of **100 ns**. What miss rate, in **percent**, is needed for an AMAT of **3 ns**?
questions.explain: 3 = 1 + m × 100 → m × 100 = 2 → m = 0.02 = **2%** (hit rate 98%). Compare the lesson's example: going from 97% to 99% hits cut AMAT from 10 to 6 cycles — small locality gains pay off a lot.

questions.q: L1: hit time 4 cycles, miss rate 10%. L2: hit time 12 cycles, local miss rate 20%. DRAM access: 200 cycles. What is the overall AMAT in cycles?
questions.explain: The formula nests: AMAT = t_L1 + m_L1 × (t_L2 + m_L2 × t_DRAM) = 4 + 0.10 × (12 + 0.20 × 200) = 4 + 0.10 × 52 = 4 + 5.2 = **9.2 cycles**. L1's miss penalty is itself the average cost of going to L2.

questions.q: A program repeatedly loops over a 2 MB array on a CPU whose largest cache is 1 MB; blocks are evicted before they are reused. What kind of misses are these?
choices: Capacity misses
Compulsory (cold) misses
Conflict misses
Write misses
questions.explain: The **working set** (2 MB) is larger than the cache, so blocks are evicted before reuse — **capacity** misses. **Compulsory** misses are the unavoidable first touch of each block; **conflict** misses happen when the cache has room overall but placement rules force hot blocks into the same set.

questions.q: In a direct-mapped cache that is mostly empty, a loop alternates between `x[i]` and `y[i]`, whose addresses happen to map to the same cache line. Nearly every access misses. What kind of misses are these?
choices: Conflict misses (thrashing)
Capacity misses
Compulsory misses
Spatial misses
questions.explain: The cache has plenty of room, but the placement rule (direct-mapped: each block has exactly one possible line) forces both hot blocks into the same slot, so they keep evicting each other — **conflict** misses, also called *thrashing*. Set-associativity reduces this.

questions.q: A **64 KB**, **4-way** set-associative cache has **64-byte** lines. How many sets does it have?
questions.explain: Capacity C = S × E × B → S = C / (E × B) = 65,536 / (4 × 64) = **256 sets**. That means s = 8 set-index bits and b = 6 block-offset bits.

questions.q: A 32 KB, 8-way cache with 64-byte lines has 64 sets (6 offset bits, 6 set-index bits). For the address **0x0000ABCD**, what is the **set index** (in decimal)?
questions.explain: Offset = low 6 bits; set index = next 6 bits. (0xABCD >> 6) & 0x3F: 0xABCD = 1010 1011 1100 1101. Dropping the low 6 bits (00 1101 → offset 13) leaves 10 1010 1111; its low 6 bits are 10 1111 = **47**. The remaining bits (0xA) are the tag, compared against the tags of the 8 lines in set 47.

questions.q: Why does a **direct-mapped** cache not need a replacement policy?
choices: Each block can go in exactly one line, so on a miss there is only one possible victim
It never evicts anything
It always uses LRU in hardware automatically
It stores every block in every line
questions.explain: Replacement policies only matter when there's a **choice** of victim — in set-associative or fully associative caches. In a direct-mapped cache (E = 1) the incoming block's set has a single line, so that line is evicted.

questions.q: A fully associative cache holds **3 lines** and starts empty. The block access sequence is `A, B, C, A, B, D, A, B`. Using **LRU** replacement, how many **hits** occur?
questions.explain: A m, B m, C m (cold) → [A B C]. A **hit** (recency B C A). B **hit** (C A B). D miss → evict least recent **C** → [A B D]. A **hit**, B **hit**. Total **4 hits**, 4 misses. LRU kept A and B because they were used recently.

questions.q: Same cache (3 lines, fully associative, empty) and same sequence `A, B, C, A, B, D, A, B`, but with **FIFO** replacement. How many **hits** occur?
questions.explain: A m, B m, C m → queue [A B C]. A hit, B hit (hits don't change FIFO order). D miss → evict oldest **A** → [B C D]. A miss → evict B → [C D A]. B miss → evict C → [D A B]. Total **2 hits**. FIFO evicted the heavily reused A just because it was loaded first — how FIFO "punishes temporal locality."

questions.q: With a 2-line fully associative cache and the sequence `P, Q, P, R, Q, P`, LRU produces more hits than FIFO.
questions.explain: LRU: P m, Q m, P hit, R m (evict Q), Q m (evict P), P m (evict R) → **1 hit**. FIFO: P m, Q m, P hit, R m (evict P, oldest), Q **hit**, P m (evict Q) → **2 hits**. LRU usually wins when there's strong temporal locality, but it is **not** guaranteed to beat FIFO on every sequence.

questions.q: Match the weakness to the policy: which policy is simple to implement but may evict a line that is still heavily used just because it was loaded long ago?
choices: FIFO
LRU
Random
Direct-mapped
questions.explain: **FIFO** evicts by load age, ignoring use. **LRU** rewards temporal locality but is complex. **Random** needs zero tracking (fast — the slides suggest it for L1) but is unpredictable and can't be optimized for.

questions.q: Why is true LRU expensive to implement in hardware, especially in highly associative caches?
choices: It must track the full usage order of every line in a set and update it on every access, hits included
It requires reading every line from DRAM on each eviction
It needs a random-number generator per set
It requires writing all dirty lines back on every hit
questions.explain: An 8-way set has 8! = 40,320 possible orderings (≥ 16 bits of state per set), updated in the critical path on every access. Real caches use approximations like **pseudo-LRU**. Random replacement needs no state and no bookkeeping on hits — why the slides call it good for L1.

choices: Filling `new_array` between writing and reading `array` may evict `array`'s lines; fix by summing right after the first loop (or merging the loops)
The loops are stride-2; fix by making them stride-1
`sum` is not reused; fix by declaring it `static`
The array is stored column-major; fix by swapping the loops
questions.explain: Temporal locality means reusing data **soon** after touching it. The middle loop touches other data that competes for cache space, so `array` may be gone by the summation. The longer (in bytes of other data touched) you wait before reuse, the less likely the data is still cached. All three loops are stride-1, so spatial locality is fine.

questions.q: In the three-loop example with N = 1,000 `int`s (4 KB per array), a real CPU with a 32 KB L1 data cache would almost certainly still find most of `array` cached at the summation.
questions.explain: Both arrays total ~8 KB, which fits comfortably in L1, so the slide's penalty is about the *pattern*. It becomes real when the data touched between uses exceeds the cache — e.g. with 10,000,000-int (40 MB) arrays the middle loop would evict every line of `array` (capacity misses).

questions.q: What is the difference between **write-through** and **write-back** caches?
choices: Write-through updates the next level on every write; write-back updates only the cache line, marks it dirty, and writes it down when evicted
Write-through writes to the disk; write-back writes to registers
Write-back is used only in SSDs
Write-through skips the cache entirely on reads
questions.explain: Write-through is simple but generates bus traffic on every store. **Write-back** (the modern norm) saves bus traffic at the cost of tracking **dirty** lines. On a write miss, a **write-allocate** cache first loads the line (typically paired with write-back) — which is why `array[i] = i;` brings `array` into the cache for the following read loop.

questions.q: In modern byte-addressable memory, why does byte order (endianness) need to be decided at all?
choices: Each address holds one byte, but most values span several bytes, so the system must decide which byte goes at the lowest address
Each address holds one bit, so bits must be ordered
Hex digits must be ordered within each byte
Caches store bytes in random order
questions.explain: Each address names **1 byte (8 bits)**. A 4-byte `int` or 8-byte `long` occupies several consecutive addresses, and the order of its bytes relative to the lowest address is its **endianness**.

questions.q: The 32-bit value **0xCAFEF00D** is stored at addresses 0x100–0x103 on a **little-endian** machine. What are the bytes at 0x100, 0x101, 0x102, 0x103?
choices: 0D F0 FE CA
CA FE F0 0D
D0 0F EF AC
F0 0D CA FE
questions.explain: Little endian puts the **least significant byte** (0D) at the lowest address, then F0, FE, and the MSB CA last. Endianness reverses **bytes**, never the hex digits inside a byte — so 0D stays 0D (option 3 wrongly reverses nibbles). Big endian would store CA FE F0 0D.

questions.q: A little-endian machine holds the bytes `EF BE AD DE` at addresses 0x200–0x203. What 32-bit value (in hex) is stored there?
questions.explain: Read the bytes right-to-left (highest address = MSB), keeping each byte's digits intact: DE AD BE EF → **0xDEADBEEF**.

questions.q: A little-endian machine stores a 16-bit unsigned value as the bytes `10 27` (at addresses 0x00, 0x01). What is the value in **decimal**?
An 8-byte `long` holding **5** is accidentally read as a 4-byte `int` (the first four bytes at its address). What value is read on a big-endian vs. a little-endian machine?
choices: Big endian: 0; little endian: 5
Big endian: 5; little endian: 0
Both read 5
Both read 0
questions.explain: Big endian stores `00 00 00 00 00 00 00 05`; the first four bytes are all zero → **0**. Little endian stores `05 00 00 00 00 00 00 00`; the first four bytes `05 00 00 00`, read LSB-first, are **5**. In little endian the value's address points at its low-order end, so a shorter read keeps the low-order part.

questions.q: An 8-byte `long` holding **0x0000000100000007** is misread as a 4-byte `int` from its starting address on a **little-endian** machine. What decimal value is read?
questions.explain: Little-endian bytes: `07 00 00 00 01 00 00 00`. The first four (`07 00 00 00`) give 0x00000007 = **7**, silently losing the upper half (the value 2³² + 7 doesn't fit in 32 bits). Little endian's "truncated read still works" advantage only holds **when the value fits in the smaller type**. (Big endian would read `00 00 00 01` = 1.)

questions.q: Which operations are cited as easier or faster with **little-endian** byte order? Select all that apply.
choices: Increments, addition, and subtraction
Checking whether a number is even or odd
Checking the sign bit
Comparing magnitudes byte-by-byte like `memcmp`
Reading a memory dump as a human
questions.explain: Little endian puts the LSB at the lowest address, so multi-byte addition proceeds with increasing addresses as the carry flows upward, and parity lives in the byte at the base address. **Big endian** makes the sign-bit check, byte-wise magnitude comparison, and human reading of dumps easy, because the MSB comes first.

questions.q: Converting a value from big-endian to little-endian reverses the order of the hex digits (e.g. 0x1234 becomes 0x4321).
questions.explain: Endianness reorders whole **bytes**, not nibbles or bits: 0x1234 is stored as `12 34` (big) or `34 12` (little). Reading it as 0x4321 is a classic mistake.

questions.q: Two hosts exchange a 32-bit integer over TCP/IP: a little-endian x86 sender and a big-endian receiver. What is the standard way to avoid misreading the value?
choices: Convert to network byte order (big endian) with `htonl` before sending, and back with `ntohl` after receiving
Nothing — TCP automatically detects each host's endianness
Always send values as 4 separate 1-bit fields
Convert everything to little endian, the network standard
questions.explain: Mismatched byte order must be translated by the OS, software, or libraries. Internet protocols use **network byte order = big endian**. `htons`/`htonl` (host-to-network) and `ntohs`/`ntohl` (network-to-host) are no-ops on big-endian hosts and byte swaps on little-endian ones, so the same code is correct everywhere.

choices: 1 — x86 is little endian, so the byte at x's lowest address is the LSB (01)
0 — x86 is big endian, so the MSB (00) is at the lowest address
1 — the cast always reads the least significant byte regardless of endianness
It depends on the compiler, not the hardware
questions.explain: `p` points at the byte at x's **lowest address**. On little-endian hardware (x86, x86-64, ARM as normally configured, RISC-V) that's the LSB, `01`. On a big-endian machine (IBM Z, classic 68000/SPARC) it would be `00`. This is the classic runtime endianness test.

questions.q: Where do the terms *big endian* and *little endian* come from?
choices: Jonathan Swift's *Gulliver's Travels* (1726), where Lilliputians war over which end of a boiled egg to crack; Danny Cohen brought the terms into computing in 1980
Two rival 1970s chip companies, Big Endian Inc. and Little Endian Ltd.
The order of bits in Morse code
IBM's naming scheme for its System/360 mainframes
questions.explain: Big-Endians cracked the big end, Little-Endians the little end — Swift satirizing bloodshed over a trivial difference. Cohen's IEN 137, *"On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace,"* made the same point about byte order: either works, **what matters is that everyone agrees**.

questions.q: Why do the slides say a C++ `long` "may be 4 or 8 bytes depending on the system"?
choices: 64-bit Linux/macOS use the LP64 model (long = 8 bytes) while 64-bit Windows uses LLP64 (long = 4 bytes)
`long` changes size depending on the value stored in it
Big-endian systems use 8-byte longs and little-endian systems 4-byte longs
The size depends on how much RAM is installed
questions.explain: Type sizes follow the platform's **data model**, which is independent of endianness. `int` is 4 bytes virtually everywhere; `long` is 8 on LP64 and 4 on LLP64. Use `<cstdint>` types like `int64_t` when the exact size matters — and size mismatches are exactly how the long-read-as-int bug happens.

questions.q: When does endianness actually matter in practice?
choices: When data moves between systems (machines, files, network protocols) that may use different byte orders — then something must translate
On every arithmetic instruction, which must check endianness first
Only when a program uses floating-point numbers
Only on machines with more than 4 GB of RAM
questions.explain: Within one consistent system the choice is unimportant. It matters at boundaries: network protocols (big endian), file formats that fix or mark their order (UTF-16 byte-order mark `FE FF` / `FF FE`, TIFF's `MM`/`II`), and bi-endian or mixed hardware. The OS, libraries, or format specs handle the translation.
